utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Good afternoon to everybody in the courtroom. If there is nothing to raise before the witness enters the court, the witness should be brought in, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Excuse me, we were dealing with some technical matters here on the bench. Welcome back to the Tribunal. May I remind you that the affirmation to tell the truth still applies. And Mr. Tolimir has further questions for you. Mr. Tolimir, please continue your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. May there be peace in this house and may God's will be done in these proceedings, and may the outcome be as God wishes and not as I wish it. And I wish you a pleasant and comfortable stay in this courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Yesterday, we left on talking about the agreement of the 24th of July, 1995 and you voiced certain suspicions about Mr. Hamdija Torlak being the authorised person to sign the agreement and the agreement that then would be binding on the army; is that correct? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: The answer to the question is: I can't answer affirmative to the word "suspicions." I don't know if that was translation but I wouldn't use the word "suspicion". What I would say is when Viktor Bezruchenko and I left Sarajevo, we did so understanding that there was some sort of capitulation by the Bosnian or Bosniak side. That's clear in the reports from David Harland when he said, I sent them. I then sent them. It was after getting that news. Second, we stopped by Lukavica barracks and met with the Serb liaison officer Major Indjic, who further conveyed the terms of that the agreement, so we were aware of that agreement, but I repeat what I said yesterday, that while we were aware that there was some form of capitulation, we were not acting pursuant to that document or in implementation of that document and I underscore what I said yesterday that specifically with respect to the demilitarisation provision, we -- that was not our priority and that was not on our agenda. Absolutely not. The priority was to address this safe movement of the population, and further, the reporting shows that both the document and the question of modalities for handing over weapons were -- continued to be a source of dispute among the parties in Sarajevo. And finally, just if the Chamber would permit, just to clarify this, to make it very simple. It all makes a great deal of sense. The priority had to be, first, the modalities for moving the population before you could get to weapons, because no armed group was going to surrender its weapons until it was assured of its security. So it was -- it simply could not have been an issue. Then, finally, to just completely wrap it up, this question, at no time, while we were in Zepa, do I recall now anyone, either Serb or Bosnians or Bosniak or UN, ever raising or discussing the issue with us of, oh, well, gee, where are their weapons, we need to start collecting weapons. I simply do not recall that. We were focused again, Your Honours, we were focused on this safe movement of the population. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Yesterday in one of your answers, or maybe it was a misinterpretation for me, that was on page 26, lines 17 through 25, and I quote: "What has to be stressed here is that the provision on demilitarisation, as far as I know, is not valid. It was an agreement that was signed by a civilian representative, at least that was my understanding, and he was not authorised to take upon himself any obligations that had to do with armaments." And then you go on to say: "The person who was authorised in Zepa to agree with demilitarisation and handover of weapons was Colonel Pavic [as interpreted], who was a soldier as I was." So based on what I've just read, that the priority for you was not the agreement and the demilitarisation itself, my question then would be whether this agreement on demilitarisation of 1993 was actually the basis for all the subsequent agreements that were signed between Serbs and the Muslims in Zepa and Srebrenica, and did they contain a provision that there should be no military presence whatsoever in order for a zone to be considered demilitarised? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you, General Tolimir. I believe I understand the question, and my answer to that is I don't know that I'm a competent witness to state definitively what document was the basis for the UNPROFOR effort in Zepa. If you consult the reports that I -- from David Harland that have been entered into evidence, it reflects the continuing dispute in Sarajevo about the validity of this document, which was reported to General Smith, David Harland states that clearly that he reported this to General Smith. And as I mentioned, I further reported on my own to General Smith my own questions about validity of a surrender of military forces by a local civilian leader. So it's a fair question and it's a very legitimate question what document was the basis for our operation there. I understand we were there because we knew that this UN declared safe area had fallen and we knew that there had been conversation between General Mladic and General Smith, that as in Srebrenica, there was going to be an outward movement of the population. And there was keen interest on our part to do as much as we could to ensure it would be done in a humanitarian way. That's the best I can answer that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let us now take a look at D21 in e-court. This is a demilitarisation agreement for Zepa and Srebrenica in 1993, and they contain certain issues that relate to your remit, civilians and the movement of the population in that area that you mentioned. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: We see here that this is an agreement on a cease-fire on the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina concluded between Lieutenant-General Ratko Mladic and General Sefer Halilovic. And it was concluded and signed on the 8th of May, 1993, and if we can please just see where it says that it was signed.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter could not hear the date.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We should have the second page in Serbian and we can keep the same page in English. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Well, there's some error here. Thank you. Now, can you see here in paragraph 1 where it says that demilitarised zone, Article 1, "To demilitarise the areas of Srebrenica and Zepa." And then below: "The demilitarised areas will include the area within the current lines of conflict. The UNPROFOR commander will mark the precise boundaries on the ground after consultations. At a later stage, contracting parties can agree verbally, or in writing, to enlarge the demilitarised zone." And so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now, can we see page 2 of this agreement, please, and can we show the next page to the witness as well. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Now, let's take a look at Article 3, you can see it on your monitor, and it's the one on the top where it says: "Every military or paramilitary unit will have either to withdraw from the demilitarised zone or submit/hand-over their weapons. Ammunition, mines, explosives, and combat supplies in the demilitarised zones will be handed over/submitted to UNPROFOR." Thank you. "After submission/hand-over of all weapons, ammunition, mines and combat supplies in the DMZ, the contracting parties will declare that the demilitarisation is complete." Now, let's take a look at Article 4. "UNPROFOR shall take the handed-over/submitted weapons into custody." In other words, the weapons will be handed over to UNPROFOR and that will be their responsibility. And then it says: "UNPROFOR shall take the handed-over/submitted ammunition into custody separately." And so and so forth.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now have the next page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Article 5: "UNPROFOR shall control the demilitarised zone." So we see from Article 4 that the UNPROFOR was the body that was supposed to control the demilitarised zone. Now, let's see the last two paragraphs in Article 4, and it says: "Noncombatants, who are in or who are willing to enter the demilitarised zone, except members of UNPROFOR are not permitted to have in their possession any weapons, ammunition or explosives. Weapons, ammunition and explosives in their possession shall be seized by UNPROFOR. Combatants will not be allowed to enter or to be in the demilitarised zone." Can we now see the next page, please, to see the section that deals with the freedom of movement. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, at a certain point in time, you should come to a question. It takes a very long time to go through the whole document without putting any question to the witness. It will be difficult for the witness to answer a question.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Well, I will put a question now.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Did -- was it the UNPROFOR's responsibility and task to make this area demilitarised and was it supposed to keep in its custody the weapons that were surrendered rather than leave them with the soldiers? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, you should add that this document was signed in 1993.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. General Tolimir, the document speaks for itself and you've read out those core obligations and they are what they say and they do, absolutely, impose obligations on the parties and an obligation on the part of UNPROFOR and that is correct. I would just add that when Viktor Bezruchenko and I arrived in Zepa in July of 1995, this document was not -- was no longer in force. This had been completely superseded by the events. Because as you know, General, the safe area was no longer demilitarised, because there was a presence of your forces there, including with heavy weapons and, I readily acknowledge, weapons on the Armija side as well. So we know that the terms of this document were completely and utterly superseded by events on the ground when Viktor and I arrived on the scene. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. So it is your claim that this agreement was not valid, however, you always referred to it. Now, tell me this: Was the agreement on demilitarisation of 1993 binding on Colonel Pavic and did he -- was he obliged to remove or withdraw his personnel from the enclave based on this agreement on demilitarisation of 1993.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: Colonel Palic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: To answer the question, let me first clarify, I did not say that this document was not valid in the sense that -- I wouldn't compare this to the other document, for example. There's a question of the validity of the other document. This document was valid, perfectly valid. When it was signed, it was signed by a competent military authority on both sides, Mladic and Halilovic. So this document I do not say was not valid. I say it was completely superseded by events on the ground. This document was written at a time of a completely different military context and it requires demilitarisation. I say again when the two civil affairs officers arrived, myself and Viktor Bezruchenko, this was completely superseded by events on the ground. Serb forces, including with heavy weapons, had entered, and General Tolimir is absolutely correct, and the Armija had not demilitarised and yes, General Tolimir, you are correct, that was a obligation, and those obligations do speak for themselves in the document. Now, I'm not competent to explain why the provisions of this agreement signed in 1993 were not fulfilled. It would -- another witness would have to explain what transpired after 1993 up to 1995 and explain why the document and what happened on both sides that made this. So I can't answer that, I am afraid. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, during your last question you said, "however, you always referred to it." I don't understand this statement, could you explain it further?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, my apologies for being imprecise. What I meant was that the UNPROFOR always referred to this agreement. I didn't really mean the gentleman here, the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Please carry on.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Now according to what you knew while you were in Sarajevo, did UNPROFOR at any point in time take a serious position on this problem of the enclaves in Zepa and Srebrenica? Did it ever try to actually enforce the demilitarisation in Zepa? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Tolimir, I understand the question and I think that is a legitimate question, but this witness is not really able to respond to that. The question of the demilitarisation of the safe areas was always an issue and it was a question of dispute for some time, and I simply did not then, nor now, have the particular background or experience with respect to what were isolated enclaves, both Srebrenica and Zepa, and our own UN access to these through Serb-controlled territory was always difficult and I simply cannot respond, but it's a fair question.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we now please see 1D195 in e-court. This is a document produced by Mustafa Hajrulahovic also known as Talijan and it was sent to General Hadzihasanovic in the Zepa Brigade. We will see it in a moment. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: We can see the document now before us, can we just zoom in a bit. Now, you can see this document is dated the 17th of February, 1995. It was sent from the Kakanj command to General Hadzihasanovic, who was the Chief of Staff of the BH army. So General Hajrulahovic is sending this to the Chief of Staff, Hadzihasanovic, and he is also ceasing the Zepa Brigade and he says the following: "In view of the deterioration of the situation around the protected zone of Zepa, we have learned the following: The aggressor has requested from the UNPROFOR that Zepa be proclaimed a non-demilitarised zone. This request came from the aggressor and is justified by the aggressor with the fact that in the past two weeks, on several occasions, there were helicopter flights bringing weapons into Zepa. The aggressor has reported several movements of BH Army units in the general area around Zepa. The aggressor accused members of the Ukrainian Bat and UNPROFOR, who are deployed in Zepa, of concealing the activities and intentions of the BH Army in that area." And then bullet point 3: "On the 16th of February, 1995, the aggressor informed the command of Sarajevo sector of the UNPROFOR that, in the event that Zepa is not proclaimed a non-demilitarised zone, they would launch an attack within seven days. The countdown for the ultimatum is, as UNPROFOR said, begun on the 16th of February and it will expire on the 23rd of February, 1995." Now, were you aware that the VRS, and its Main Staff, as the other side is claiming here, repeatedly demanded that this zone be demilitarised so that we wouldn't have to do it ourselves? Is that clear from this document? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Tolimir, I'm not here to dispute your proposition and what you state. However, I cannot attest to this because my involvement in Zepa began only over this period of July 1995, and in general terms, I was aware that the demilitarisation of safe areas was a chronic sore point, but the explanation for that is one, is a wider and more complex, requires a more complex and longer discussion as to why that is the case, but this witness cannot answer the question of awareness of this, because my awareness of Zepa and involvement in Zepa began in July of 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Did the UNPROFOR command in Sarajevo have the obligation to be aware of this since it reads here that the aggressor forwarded the request to UNPROFOR? In other words, should not UNPROFOR have been aware of such a request having been sent to the staff? The document is dated the 17th of February, 1995. The author is the Muslim side. I didn't want to put a document to you authored by the Serbian side. I don't want to misrepresent the facts, as it were. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I understand, General Tolimir, and UNPROFOR command may well have been aware, but this witness cannot confirm that and I believe there would be other witnesses that might appear before this Chamber who could better answer that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you for your frank answer. Let us look at the legality, or lack thereof, on the part of Hamdija Torlak on the to sign the agreement on behalf of those soldiers, as you put it. In other words, did he have the requisite authority to sign the agreement, because this was an agreement enveloping military issues such as weaponry. So my question for you is, do you know what sort of role was played by Hamdija Torlak within the local authorities in Zepa who in July of 1995 negotiated with the VRS on behalf of the army of Zepa and on behalf of the Zepa enclave? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: The answer to that question is no, I and my colleague Viktor Bezruchenko did not really know the role he played. And to put it in context, we have to remember these isolated eastern enclaves, Srebrenica, Zepa, Gorazde, UNPROFOR had very little access to, so even if I had had reports from colleagues, other than Gorazde, we really had very very limited contact and understanding of the actual situation. It's possible someone else knew, but neither Viktor nor I understood exactly the structure there in Zepa, as, for example, we did in other places in Bosnia where we were permitted and had more regular access.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, I understand your point.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now show in e-court P740. I'm only interested in 25.25 to 25.50, and from 34.4 to 35.5. This is footage featuring Mr. Torlak as having been sent for negotiations by the Muslims in Zepa. Let's look at the video. I apologise, of course you needn't have known him, but let's see here whether he was a representative of Zepa or not.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Your microphone was off, Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I can see that the witness has interpretation here, I was speaking up simply because we didn't have the audio. Can we have the volume a bit higher up, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Witness, did you hear -- the individual in the white shirt, that was Hamdija Torlak, did you hear what he said?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not exactly. What did he say? I didn't -- I was looking more at the visual, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. He appeared there as a part of the Muslim delegation that we didn't have anything to do with and he said, "We agreed that the entire population should leave the safe area of Zepa." That was the line he uttered. "We agreed that the entire population should leave the protected area of Zepa?"

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we see the relevant clip yet again, and then General Kukanjac says, "We will ensure that you have safe passage across the Serb-controlled territory." This is video footage that was tendered by the Prosecution, not by me. Can the relevant part of the footage be shown to the witness again, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It would be appreciated, because we didn't hear the voice either, it was very low voice and we would like to see the relevant part again. Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. President. Just two quick points, so the record is clear and correct. The first is I see we have a reference to General Kukanjac at page 13, line 13. I'm sure General Tolimir said something else, we just need to correct that. I think we should also add, for clarity of the record, there is no dispute of about this, that this is video footage shot on the 19th of July.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Tolimir, the name of which general was mentioned by you?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I mentioned General Mladic. I don't know how it came to me mentioning General Kukanjac. I don't even know him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you for this clarification. Mr. Gajic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think I know where the problem lies. The individual we can see right now in e-court is called Kulovac, not Kukanjac, and we seem to have seen the name in the transcript quite by chance, the name is Benjamin Kulovac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Let's see the relevant part of the video again with hopefully a good audio recording.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I do hope that audibility was better this time. If not, we can do it once more.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: This was the Muslim representative, Hamdija Torlak, wearing a white shirt, who said we agreed that under the circumstances, the issue of Zepa is best resolved by having the entire population of Zepa leave the area safely. And General Mladic replies to that by saying, I don't want to cause any more suffering to you, we will allow safe passage to you. So this is my question: Based on this footage can it be seen that the gentleman wearing a white shirt over which he slung this jacket, so he is to the right of the man serving drinks, did Hamdija Torlak say that they had agreed that, under the circumstances, the most expedient solution would be for the entire population of Zepa to leave the area as -- did it not happen as Mr. Thayer said on the 19th of July?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: In answer it to your question, I was not present at this meeting and my testimony is limited to the video that this Court has seen and I can only say that I saw, watched the same video everyone else saw and it reflects what you are saying. This doesn't go to the point raised yesterday about the validity. These gentleman could have spoken in English, in legal Latin, and said it five times. The question is were they competent to enter, to surrender military forces. That's the question that we raised, and we know in Sarajevo that there were continuing disputes about their competence and their validity and that's all I can say. But I did watch this video and it is indeed, as you say, General Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now have only the individual to the right of Mr. Torlak shown. He is wearing a uniform. We can see the star and the insignia of the United Nations. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for Mr. Tolimir, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Your microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: We see an individual wearing the UNPROFOR uniform with the UN insignia, who escorted the gentleman from Zepa to the venue where negotiations took place, otherwise, they couldn't have passed on their own. And we can see the negotiations are taking place in an area where UNPROFOR was providing security. My question is this: Does the presence of UNPROFOR soldiers attest to the fact that authoritative negotiators were brought over to these negotiations, and as a follow-up, an agreement was made? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: To answer the question, again, I'll repeat, I was not present at this meeting and, yes, we can see both in this photograph the presence of the UNPROFOR Ukrainian, and I believe it was, I'm grateful it was pointed out to me yesterday that the other individual, Dudnjik, was perhaps this officer, perhaps, who is in the photograph now. I acknowledge all that, we all see that. What I'm saying is, despite that, despite that, there still could be a question as to the validity of the document, but General Tolimir, I absolutely acknowledge we see the visual evidence of the presence of UNPROFOR.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Would you perhaps know what the capacity was of Mr. Torlak when he came from Zepa to attend to these negotiations, and did he have any sort of contact or communication with Avdo Palic or any other members of the BH Army? Do you have any knowledge of that at all? Thank you?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I do not have any knowledge about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now have 1D201 shown. It's a letter sent by Alija Izetbegovic to Avdo Palic. We would only like to see the way in which Avdo Palic treats Hamdija Torlak and his role in negotiations.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: While we are waiting for this to appear, I will be quoting the basis for my question to you. Yet again, the document was not authored by the VRS but by the Muslim side. As I said, it was sent to Avdo Palic by Alija Izetbegovic. Or actually, sorry, the other way around, it was sent from Zepa, from Avdo Palic, to Sarajevo to Alija Izetbegovic. We don't have it yet. It's 1D201. There we have it. Avdo Palic writes to Alija Izetbegovic on the 27th of July. You have the English version there. It was sent on the date I mentioned at 7.00 a.m. It reads: "Mr. President, we've received both your letters and the agreement you sent us. I would like to ask you, just between the two of us, if we could keep it for our own internal use. And are you prepared to exchange all of us from Zepa, who number around 2.500, together with the people who came from Srebrenica, for all the Chetniks? Let us stress that more than half of these men do not have weapons and we have no chance of making a break-through. Please could we have your reply by 0800 hours this morning so that we may know what we are to do next, because the criminal Mladic and our representative Hamdija Torlak are still at Boksanica. One more question: Would you be prepared to pay for the helicopters needed to evacuate us should the UNPROFOR agree to this?" Signed commander Colonel Avdo Palic. This is my question, based on what I've read out to you: How does the military commander of Zepa treat Hamdija Torlak if he refers to him as our representative, and perhaps even if we find out that he was on the War Staff and I have a document to that effect. So would it not transpire, based on what I've just read out to you, that Avdo Palic is seeking instructions for the sake of his negotiator? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Tolimir, reading this letter, that may well have been the case. It may have been the case that Mr. Torlak was operating in close co-ordination and even at the direction of Colonel Palic. I'm telling you we did not know that then, nor are we certain now what that was and I'm simply repeating the point that a military surrender, a surrender of military assets, that was there was a significant question as to whether it could be done by a civilian official. And furthermore, that there was a dispute raised on one side as to the authority. But it may well have been that the two of them were operating in close communication.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have 1D201, the telegram admitted into evidence, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 1D201 receives number D171, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could we now have P736 shown in e-court for the benefit of the witness. I promised to show this document because it sets out the duties performed by Hamdija Torlak in Zepa. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. This is also a BH Army document issued by the 285th Zepa Brigade. It was issued on the 27th of July 1995 at 7.00. Oh, I'm sorry, I've been reading the previous document. So can we strike that from the record. I started reading what I thought was a new document on the screen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I was told it takes quite a long time because it is a very big document, if that is the case. Now we have a document on the screen. Is it the right document?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President, that's the document. It's a one-page document, which reads: "The War Presidency of the Zepa municipality, at its meeting held on the 27th of July, 1995, attended by Hajric" - and first name being Mehmed I believe - "president of the War Presidency; Hamdija Torlak, president of the executive committee; and Amir Tomanovic - Imamovic, sorry - commander of the civilian protection staff, hereby adopts the following decision."

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: So this is a decision that they adopted as War Presidency. It's binding on all those present in Zepa. It reads: "All the able-bodied men from -- aged 18 to 55 years shall surrender their weapons to the representatives of the Army of Republika Srpska in the presence of the UNPROFOR at the UNPROFOR base in Zepa. All the able-bodied men shall be registered by the ICRC and shall be guarded by the forces of the Army of Republika Srpska in the presence of UNPROFOR in Zepa until an agreement on an exchange -- until an agreement on the disarmament has been reached." Paragraph 2, which reads: "Urgently inform the Muslim authorities in Sarajevo about this decision and set about its implementing it forthwith. Zepa, the 27th of July, 1995. The first person signed is Rajko Kusic, who is the Rogatica Brigade commander of the VRS. It's certified by Mladic and signed on behalf of the War Presidency, by Mehmed Hajric as president of the Zepa War Presidency; Hamdija Torlak, as we said he is the member of the executive committee, and ex officio member of the War Presidency; and Amir Imamovic, as member of the War Presidency and commander of the civilian protection staff. So please answer this question I have for you: Was this document not signed by authorised individuals from Zepa and did there exist in Zepa at the time anybody who would have had higher authority than them to sign such a document? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you, General Tolimir, I understand the question and here is my answer: The document is as it reads exactly, as you say, on its face and I would have no basis to dispute this document. What I'm saying is that first of all, we didn't know the exact structure until we got there. When I said I didn't know who Hamdija Torlak was, I meant until we arrived there. We did meet with, I recall, a meeting with Mr. Torlak in which he probably told me his function and title, but this is after that -- the agreement, the one that you are referring to earlier about demilitarisation. So, yes, this document is signed by the civilian authorities, that's absolutely true. What I'm simply stating is that we had a question about the validity of that document, whether or not we were correct. Maybe we were not correct, maybe the law provides that civilians are allowed to surrender and even local civilians, not the central authority of a country. Maybe the law does provide. I doubt it. I would be surprised if that were the case because military assets are a federal national state asset and it would be surprising if a local mayor in any country could either surrender his assets or command them to go on an attack. But we could say we were wrong. Perhaps we were mistaken in that belief. The point and the value of this witness is that this question of this document was not in our minds. That's not what we were focusing on. We certainly were not focusing on any demilitarisation provision, because as you know, this was not a demilitarised zone. There were Serb weapons, heavy weapons in there as well as army weapons. So we were not looking at that. And our preoccupation and focus was with the safe onward transport of, first, the women and children, and second, if the agreement could be reached on how we would have modalities for the safe transport of the men. That's what this witness can bring to light. I was not present and really can't bring anything of value about these documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us whether the demilitarised zone in Zepa that you just mentioned contained Serbian weapons or whether those weapons were outside that zone? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: It would depend -- the answer to that would depend on what the actual perimeter was of that area, but, General Tolimir, you yourself were in the centre of Zepa. I don't recall whether you were carrying a side-arm or not, but you certainly had, at times, your soldiers with you who were armed, and so we know for a fact that your soldiers were there and we also mow that you had various artillery positions in there. I don't know now that the exact boundary, but we certainly know for a fact that there were Serb weapons inside this what would have been the demilitarised zone. And I'm acknowledging that presumably there were Armija weapons inside the zone as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Sir, can you consider me to be armed, together with my escort, if I came there after the cease-fire agreement was signed? That's one question. And the second question is, does this agreement envisage that the VRS should in any way disarm or remove their forces from the zone? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't listen to the original Serbian, so I know we have very high-quality interpreters here, and I doubt that there was a translation issue, but taken literally, the first question is, Can you consider me to be armed if I came after the cease-fire. General Tolimir, you are armed if you are carrying arms. It's irrespective of what the agreement is. And the second question, does the agreement envisage, I don't know which agreement -- if you are talking about the original agreement, the 1993 agreement, the one that you showed with -- signed between General Mladic and General Halilovic, yes, that clearly called for a demilitarised zone and demilitarised means demilitarised. Now, as I said, that was superseded, because your forces had entered Zepa and these -- these were new terms and new documents, but I'm saying again, repeating, this document and these agreements were not what we had in our minds of what we were trying to do. We were concerned, first and foremost and always, with the safe transport of, first, the women and children of Zepa, and then second, assuming there was an agreement on the men.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now have D51. And then when we have it on the screen, I'm going to ask you a question based on what you just said.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Does the UNPROFOR have the right to change any of the paragraphs in an agreement that was agreed upon by the warring factions? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand the question. I'd have to have an explanation of what that question is about.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Here we can see the agreement on the disarmament of the able-bodied population in the Zepa enclave. So we are now talking about the able-bodied population of the Zepa enclave. So this was an agreement about them disarming. My question is, can the UNPROFOR change anything that is written in this agreement, I'm being very specific here. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And this is the agreement of the 24th of July, 1995.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, thank you for intervening because I was about to appeal to you and Your Honours there. I've repeated what my -- what I'm able to speak to and I'm simply not able to speak to these documents or the issues that the accused is trying to raise. I simply can't. I've testified repeatedly that our mindset, what we were focused on was the -- this movement of safe, as safe and humane as possible movement. And the validity or non-validity of these document, yes, there was a question in our minds, but I can't speak to what UNPROFOR can change or not change. I cannot really attest to validity of communications between the Armija. I just simply state that for the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. After having received this answer several times, I think you should move to another part of your questioning.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: You stated yesterday about that the agreement dated the 24th of July, you said that you returned to Zepa on the 25th of July, 1995, which is the day after the signing of this agreement. Can you answer this question: What was the purpose of your arrival to Zepa? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: My understanding of what our mission was, was to help co-ordinate the movement of the population of Zepa and to do so, of course, in as safe and humane way co-ordinating with all the relevant parties, that would be the Serbs and the VRS of course; the Bosnians or Bosniaks, the Armija and their civilian leadership as well; and plus the UNPROFOR assets that were there, the Ukrainians, and the UNPROFOR assets that would come; and any other humanitarian organisation that would come, such as ICRC, and normally UNHCR, but UNHCR refused to participate in this. So that was our role. I do not recall that we had specific instructions or directions and I certainly do not recall that we had the instruction to implement this agreement that Torlak had signed, and I don't recall any conversation at all including before we left about the demilitarisation provision. I don't recall any conversation about that which is unusual because had there been -- had that been something that was appreciated as a real obligation, then of course we would have had discussions about that, but we had none. So it was really the focus, General Tolimir, was on this safe movement of the population, co-ordinating that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now have D55. That is the report drafted by Viktor Bezruchenko entitled, "The fall of Zepa." Mr. Bezruchenko was there together with Mr. Edward. We are interested in 98 and 99, paragraph 98 and paragraph 99. Can we have it on the screens. Okay. Now I think we are going to get it on the screens. It's page 27 in Serbian and 26 in English. Thank you, Aleksandar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Just for the record, the current witness is Mr. Joseph. Mr. Edward Joseph and not Mr. Edward.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: All right. Now we can see the paragraph that I'm interested in. It goes as follows, I quote: These are the words of Mr. Bezruchenko: "The UNPROFOR updated situation report for 24th and 25th July confirmed that the negotiations between the parties were completed at 1930 hours on the 24th July. The report describes the negotiations and agreement as follows." Now I'm going to quote what it says in English: "At 1930, the negotiations between both WFs were completed, it was agreed to evacuate children, women and old men and injured Muslims from the Zepa pocket to the safe areas. Wounded people are to be transported to Sarajevo by UKRCOY trucks. The UKRCOY. At 2030, BiH side accepted the following BSA demands: 1, to put all equipment and weapons under UNPROFOR control. 2, to clear all the roads from mines. To evacuate the local population from Zepa town. UNPROFOR representatives from SHQ Sarajevo are going to arrive at Zepa town on the 25th of July at 0800 hours." So this is what Mr. Bezruchenko says. Further on, in paragraph 99, he says: "The agreement was validated by signature block of General Mladic. The full text of the agreement was sent to the VRS Main Staff by the 1st Podrinje Light Infantry Brigade commander Kusic on the 24th of July." So having read this, we can see that you and Viktor knew of this agreement and that you arrived there pursuant to provisions of this agreement in order to perform certain tasks. Did the UNPROFOR try to negate this agreement in any way or did they try to change any of the provisions of the agreement, the provisions as they were stipulated in the agreement itself? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Tolimir, first we can see that my colleague Viktor Bezruchenko is quoting reports and he is presumably correctly quoting these reports, so it's not Viktor is not saying when Ed Joseph and I entered Zepa, we had it in our mind to work on demilitarisation. He is not saying that, he is simply citing the record presumably correctly, that's number 1. Number 2, it's already been entered into the record that Viktor and I did know about this agreement. We did know this. Remember? We were briefed on this by Major Indjic, your liaison officer back in Sarajevo, Serb Sarajevo before we went back there. And our colleague, David Harland, had also been made aware, so yes, we were aware of this and with respect to UNPROFOR negating or not negating, I can only tell you it's moot issue, or it was not a ripe, issue because we could never get, it was never any question for us of demilitarising at that point, because we had to first establish the basis for safe transport of the women and children and then to figure out what would be done with the men. And at no point do I recall - Viktor and I, we were in close proximity there throughout this period in Zepa - do I ever recall a conversation with Viktor about, Gee, how are we going to take care of mines, and, Gee, where are we going to collect the weapons. It just simply never came up, as far as I can recall 15 and a half years later.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. So if you and Viktor only took care of the evacuation of the population, does that mean that the military commander or somebody else should have taken care of those weapons? Then who was in charge of the weapons, when I say weapons, I mean the weapons that belonged to the warring parties? Was it then in the hands or jurisdiction of the civilian sector or of the military sector? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Tolimir, hopefully you'll have a chance to pose that question to a leadership of the then UNPROFOR military command. I can recall, and this would be very unusual for us as civil affairs officers not to be aware of such a development, but I don't recall within UNPROFOR having any conversation about it. And further, General Tolimir, I don't recall you and I ever having a conversation about it or General Mladic and myself and Mr. Bezruchenko having a conversation about it. Although, we did at times, certainly with General Mladic, discuss the question of the potential movement of the men of Zepa.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Joseph. Was I under any obligation to discuss those issues with you? I or General Mladic? We are talking about an agreement here, does that mean that we had a duty to brief you on it?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, you had no such obligation.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. This agreement dated the 24th of July, which was the basis for your arrival for performing civilian tasks was signed by Mr. Dudnjik, he was the commander of the Ukrainian company of the UNPROFOR stationed in Zepa. My question is: Was anybody else in Zepa in a more authorised position than him to sign this agreement and to take upon himself the obligations that pertained to the UNPROFOR? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: The question of his authority to witness or be a party to such an agreement certainly where there were obligations on UNPROFOR, the question of his authorisation is one you would have to check with military -- members of the military chain. That's first of all. Second, is to put it in some context, let's have some sympathy for this Ukrainian officer who is in the middle of a very difficult situation, and where there is bombardment and bullets flying around, and it's quite possible for them, whether targeted or not, to become casualties. And so let's have some sympathy here, perhaps I have no idea whether he gained authorisation or had authorisation, but one can readily understand in the difficult environment in which they were in, that they would move and seek any chance to advance any kind of calming of the situation and of course that would -- if it would achieve some, a cessation in hostilities, of course, that is to the good. That's in the overall objectives of the UN.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know whether Mr. Dudnjik, as the UNPROFOR commander in Zepa, whether he contacted his commander in Sarajevo in order to appraise himself of whatever was agreed and whatever his tasks were? Do you maybe know that and whether -- do you maybe know whether he was supposed to do something like that? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether he did that. I would presume that he would and should notify his chain of command particularly when there would be obligations and responsibilities on the part of UNPROFOR and one would presume, assuming he had the means, that he would have done so. Perhaps he did, perhaps he did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. A moment ago I quoted the words of Mr. Bezruchenko who was there with you. He said that the Ukrainian battalion confirmed it and then you arrived based on this information that came from Zepa. So does that mean that you were invited by the Muslim side or did the UNPROFOR inform you of this agreement and invite you, I'm talking about your command who then actually sent you in the field? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe the record shows that David Harland sent us back, and I recall as well that General Smith had initially wanted civilian affairs and directed us to go. Now, whether that was the first time we went or the second, I can't be sure. But the key point here and the key player in our going to Zepa is, of course, General Tolimir, your side, because without the agreement and the approval of the Serb side, it was impossible for UN personnel such as myself to - and Viktor Bezruchenko, it was impossible for us to cross through Serb lines and many many Serb check-points without that permission from your side, which is one reason why these enclaves were so isolated.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Joseph, can you now take a look at 65 ter 07203. That's your statement. I would like to see paragraphs 10 and 11. Thank you. Okay. Now we have the paragraphs I'm interested in, 10 and 11. You can read it for yourself, I'm not going to read it out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: May I interrupt you for a short moment. I would like to clarify something in the record in the last answer, page 30, line 1. I would like to read the sentence and ask the witness if he feels himself recorded correctly. "But the key point here and the key player in our going to Zepa is, of course, General Tolimir, your side because without the agreement and the approval of the Serb side it was impossible for UN personnel and so on to move." Is that what you said?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. And the key player was not literally General Tolimir - I was addressing General Tolimir - it was the Serb side. The key player -- the key player in our being able to reach Zepa was the Serb side because they controlled the access and we -- these isolated Srebrenica Zepa Gorazde, our access was totally 100 per cent at the behest of the Serb side. That was the point, but I was not, thank you for pointing this out, I was not trying to place that in the person of General Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: If we would put a comma after the words, "is of course, General Tolimir, your side," would that be a correct recording of your words?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That would be correct. This is a deficiency in the English language. In Serbian, they have the vokativ, so it would have been clear, but we don't have that in English. Thank you, Mr. President, for clarifying that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Now, Mr. Tolimir, your question to the document on the screen.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: When you arrived in Zepa, were you accommodated in the Ukrainian Battalion base in Zepa? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we were.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. And did the evacuation of the wounded people and the part of the population begin even before you arrived there? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's possible some individuals had already been moved out, but the main part of the evacuation did not start until the following morning after we had arrived the day prior.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, let us take a look at paragraph 14, I will quote: "Evacuation started the same morning when several Serb-owned buses and trucks arrived to the centre. We started to organise the civilians boarding in the vehicles. I, Viktor, and at least one French officer, were very active on this as well as some of the Muslim civilian leaders. I can recall seeing also General Smith there observing the evacuation." My question is as follows: Did the VRS, in any way, limit the evacuation of civilians stipulated by the agreement and monitored by Viktor and, as you put it here, another French officer and the representatives of the Muslim civilian leadership? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: The answer to the question is we had no interruption or interference with respect to the -- to the movement of the women and children of Zepa, that's number 1. Number 2, I just to point out for the Chamber that it says the same morning. This would have been using the reconstruction of the record, this would have been the morning of the 26th of July. We would have arrived on the 25th. So this is reaffirming what I said was my memory that the main movement started that morning, early that morning of what I understand now was the 26th of July. But to answer your question, General Tolimir, no, there was no interference to the movement of the women and children. Again, this proceeded for us, at least, perhaps not for you, but for us proceeded without reference to any -- to this written agreement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, we must have our first break. We are over time already. We must have our first break now and we will resume quarter past 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tolimir, please continue your examination.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Before the break we talked about paragraph 14 and you said that the evacuation had begun on that very morning and you so on and so forth. Now, let's take a look at paragraph 16 of this statement of yours which reads as follows: "We compiled lists of all evacuees, and as far as I can recall, we had a separate list for each vehicle. I handed over those lists later on either to the UNHCR or someone from the UNPROFOR. We also tried to place one UNPROFOR soldier on each vehicle, but I'm not sure that we managed to do that all the time during the evacuation." Then paragraph 17: "The evacuation lasted probably three days or a little longer. The atmosphere was very tense throughout but we managed to get all those people on board who had come to the centre and were willing to go, and I estimated that approximately 7.000 people were evacuated." My question is this: Did any member of the VRS in Zepa or on the roads out of Zepa try to prevent the evacuation or the way that people were put on board buses with escorts and so on? So did anyone try it to restrict your actions or prevent you from doing any of this? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: To answer the question, General Tolimir, if the question focuses just on within the village there in Zepa, the answer is no, no member of the VRS impeded us in our work or impeded the movement. You mentioned on the outside of Zepa, if I understood correctly, and you know, of course, there were the men that you and I had discussed, lightly wounded, and my understanding, I wasn't present, of course, but my understanding was that that vehicle, that bus was stopped by Serb military personnel and that those men were taken off. I wasn't present for that, but that's my understanding. But the first part of the question, no, there was no interference in the movement of the women and children from there in the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. This is the second time that you mention the bus with the lightly wounded, or the wounded men. Let's clear something up here, do you recall whether these people were sent -- whether these people were returned from Zepa or actually from the line of separation? Thank you. Whether they were sent back?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know where they were removed from the bus. My -- what I was later told was, and I presume this was someone who told me from UNPROFOR military, I can't remember that specific detail, but what I recall being told is that at some point in the movement of that vehicle from Zepa towards the line, at some point they were stopped by Serb military personnel who boarded the vehicle and despite the presence of UNPROFOR soldier and presumably the UNPROFOR APC that I had asked to follow the vehicle, that despite that UN UNPROFOR presence, these men were pulled off. That is what I was told. Of course, I wasn't there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now, let's see paragraph 19 of this statement that we have before us. Please take a look at it and I would appreciate if we were shown the same paragraph in the Serbian version as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: You say the following: "The previously mentioned group of lightly wounded Muslims boarded probably the last bus. I recall them being a group of 12 men. As they were of military age, and therefore falling within the group of problem evacuees, I and Viktor went to VRS, General Tolimir was in the centre, down-town area. I asked him if he allowed these 12 men to go through the Serb controlled territory without being disturbed and he very emphatically replied with a yes." Now, tell us please, is this the incident that you mentioned, that you actually referred to when you spoke a little earlier about these men being taken off? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is in that context. This is those individuals, yes. These are the individuals that I'm speaking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Later, you go on to say that: "The bus departed with the wounded men and because I was still concerned for their safety, I asked a French officer, probably a major, to follow the bus with his APC which he did. Later on I heard from a source, which I cannot identify, that the bus had been stopped and the wounded men arrested." Thank you. Now, is this a reference to this same incident that you spoke about a little earlier?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Now, this officer who escorted the bus, did he report to you after the fact and did he tell you where the bus was intercepted and when?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall that detail. I only recall being told that it was stopped by Serb military and Serb military personnel boarded the bus and took them off. That's what I recall being told.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now see P736, please. We had seen it a little earlier, this is a decision of the War Presidency on disarming.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: While we wait for it to come up, let me say that it was signed on the 27th of July and the authorities in Sarajevo were supposed to be briefed on its contents and it was to be implemented. That is what is said in paragraph 2. Now, my question based on what you had occasion to see and we see that this is a document that was signed on the 27th of July, was this incident with the wounded men, did that happen on the 27th of July? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: It might well have been the 27th of July. I don't understand the connection to this document, but it might well have been the 27th of July that this occurred. It's quite possible that that was the date.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Are you aware that the president of the War Presidency, Mehmed Hajric took this document immediately, as stated in paragraph 2, to the mountains, the Zepa mountain, to brief or inform, on the content of the document, the soldiers, the troops who were deployed there? Were you aware of this, in view of the fact that you were in Zepa?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't believe I was aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Were you aware that Mr. Mehmed Hajric came back from the Zepa mountains and that he then advised the Serb side that the Muslim soldiers were not willing to surrender? Were you advised of this and -- you and the UNPROFOR representatives who were at the Zepa compound?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot recall whether or not we were advised of this. What I recall is that we were very clear that there had been no agreement reached on this prisoner exchange in Sarajevo that would permit this movement. That's what I recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know that the commander of this operation after the soldiers decided that they wouldn't act in agreement with this decision, that the commander then decided that everyone who was found on the buses should be sent back and exchanged because the brigade was not willing to surrender, that the evacuation was thereby actually terminated? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Sorry, I didn't see you. Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. It may be helpful if General Tolimir has a name in mind when he refers to "the commander of this operation," to just specify who he is talking about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Mr. Thayer had the same remark and the same question when I referred to the same operation and I was referring to the Zepa commander who was in charge of the overall operation and he was --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the accused kindly repeat his question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, I have to interrupt you. At the moment you are -- your words are not interpreted. There was a mistake and the interpreters asked you to repeat your question. Please do that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Sir, were you aware while you were in Zepa as well as the UNPROFOR commander, that because of the breaches of the agreement by the combatants, the implementation of this agreement was terminated and was this related -- relayed to you and to the Muslims and everyone who was in Zepa at the time? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Tolimir, I think I've testified here repeatedly that we were not under the impression that we were acting in furtherance of this specific agreement or -- to the contrary, we understood that there was to agreement, no agreement about the fate of the men of Zepa. That's what we understood. We did not believe that when we went in there, quite to the contrary, that we had a step-by-step understanding between the sides and we UNPROFOR would monitor and carry out our obligation to see that this step-by-step comprehensive understanding would be fully realised. No, to the contrary, we understood the crucial component of this, the fate of these men and its linkage to a prisoner exchange was undecided and so that was a huge question mark. So when I approached you to ask permission for these men, it was simply on the basis of an -- that we had an on-going movement of the women and children that had proceeded well and that, yes, that without as I've testified, without interference from the Serb military and it was in that context that I approached you and sought your permission because these lightly wounded men had asked me, repeatedly, to be moved out along with the women and children. And it was in that context and it was without reference to this document or some other obligation or something like that. And it was in that context, General Tolimir, that I approached you about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. You said a moment ago "men", why do you keep using the term "men"? Why don't you say soldiers of the Zepa Brigade, because they were soldiers, they were armed as we will see from Bezruchenko's report and Bezruchenko was with you?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it's reasonable to say -- to raise the point as to who was a soldier or, under Geneva Conventions, a combatant and who was a male civilian non-combatant. For us, as UN personnel, what was our primary concern? Our primary concern was the safety and security of everyone and we knew that any male would be presumed by your side, any male Bosniak would be presumed by your side to be a military soldier simply by being a male of military age. And, of course, it's quite ironic you mention this document signed by Mr. Hajric who was the -- both the hodza and the mayor, and, of course, that would suggest he was a non-military and a non-combatant, and my understanding is, of course, he went missing, and his body was only recently discovered to have been killed and located not too far from Zepa.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Bless his soul. I'm not happy that he was found murdered. But can you see from this document that he signed this document as a vice-president of the War Presidency and did you know that in Bosnia, Alija Izetbegovic, as the president of the Presidency, was the Commander-in-Chief and that he issued commands to the military commander and that he had powers over the military forces there? Did you know that?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would presume that Alija Izetbegovic as president of what was then known as the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina would have had those powers. I don't believe Mr. Hajric would have had those powers, but that's an issue that other lawyers can debate. My concern was for the safety of all of those men of Zepa, and as well the women and children.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we now see D54, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Because I would like you to believe what you are saying that you doubt because -- well, as we wait for this to come up, I would like to show you this document where we see the name of Mr. Hajric mentioned as the president of the War Presidency. So this is D54. We can see on the top of the page Mehmed Effendi Hajric, president of Zepa, protected. He is sending this to Alija Izetbegovic on the 19th of July, 1995, in other words, he is addressing him directly, and he says, "In response to your questions of last night," which would suggest that he the president had put some questions to him, and then under 2, it says: "An evacuation is possible only by land under the supervision of UNPROFOR. I am in contact with General Smith every day. The Chetniks are dragging out the talks on purpose. General Smith is guaranteeing the security of women and children." And so on and so forth. So that's paragraph 2, but my question will be this for you: Can you infer from this paragraph 2 that Mr. Izetbegovic had told Hajric that he was -- he accepted and agreed to the evacuation and that he was informing him of that decision in this?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Doing my best to answer this question, I am afraid I can't make that same inference, but I am not disputing that President Izetbegovic had overall authority of his forces, but I don't see the inference reflected in paragraph 2, I am afraid.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Is this addressed to Palic or Hajric, and who is it to whom he is saying, "An evacuation is possible only by land, and I am in contact with General Smith every day. The Chetniks are dragging out the talks on purpose. General Smith is guaranteeing the security of women and children," end of quote. Can you please comment on this?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I understand now, thank you, General, you are underscoring the fact that this communication is from President Izetbegovic to Hajric and I understand, I understand. It does appear on its face that President Izetbegovic is aware. Now, I have not studied this in detail and I certainly was not aware of this communication at the time, so that's really as much as I can say. I'm just -- was raising the question of the men and our communication about them. This -- I was completely unaware of this communication between these two gentlemen.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Is it not the case that Alija Izetbegovic is herein giving his consent to Palic -- Hajric, that evacuation may commence and that guarantees are given for the safety of women and children? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay. Reading this document it appears that President Izetbegovic is acknowledging here the, where is it, is acknowledging that General Smith of UNPROFOR guarantees the security of the women and children, that he is acknowledging that he has an assurance from General Smith, the commander of the UNPROFOR BH command about the women and children, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Does this mean that once an overall assessment was made, both Alija and Hajric were able to make a decision to evacuate women and children, and was this decision then relayed to Hajric or Palic? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: This communication is to Hajric and pertains to the women and children, yes. I don't see anything in there about approval of demilitarisation or other things that we've talked about, but, yeah, this communication is from President Izetbegovic to Hajric about -- and it mentions Smith's approval of the -- Smith's assurances about the movement of the women and children.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. My question didn't have to do with demilitarisation, perhaps the interpretation was wrong. What I said was: Was it Alija who gave his consent for the evacuation of women and children and not demilitarisation, because it clearly says that men should not surrender themselves? I think that's clearly stated in item 3.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: It does appear -- what it's saying literally, we are all reading the same document. I had no awareness at the time and I'm not able to provide any special knowledge than any of us here together reading this document. And, yes, this document, as I read it, as anyone here can read it, the writer of this document, President Izetbegovic is acknowledging that he has assurances from General Smith, UNPROFOR commander, about the security of women and children, and one can infer that he has no objection to the women and children being moved out. I think we can all see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: I do understand your point. You don't want to use this first word in item 2 which is "evacuation". But let's look at item 3 to see what Alija Izetbegovic had to say. I'm quoting from item 3: "My plan, move out as many civilians as possible, all if possible. The troops stay on and continue to resist. We will do all to help you by supplying materiel and technical equipment, volunteers, and, three, offensive action in your direction. I believe that this is starting today. If we do not succeed in this, you try to break out along those roads, (you know which), but now without the burden of women and children who would in the meantime be taken out." My question for you, does Mr. Izetbegovic not state clearly here to Mr. Hajric that women and children should be pulled out of Srebrenica and Zepa, whereas the soldiers should try and break through and by stating this, did he not give his consent for the evacuation of women and children?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, with respect to your comment that I don't want to use the word "evacuation", I'm fine with using the word evacuation as long as its understood in this Chamber that that does not connote an operation that did not have a military objective to it. In other words, it's fine. I'll say evacuation, exclusively, as long as its understood that that purpose was not humanitarian in nature as I testified yesterday, because our role was humanitarian in nature, the UN role was humanitarian. That is, in this difficult situation to preserve human life and to try to make it as humane as possible, but I do not believe that the actual movement was humanitarian in nature. To the contrary. But I'm happy to use that word, as long as that's understood, and it doesn't connote something else. To your second -- the other part of the question, does he give his consent? One can infer that President Izetbegovic is giving his consent to this movement or if you insist, the evacuation of the women and children. One can infer that reasonably. Again we didn't know this, had no awareness of this at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, I wanted to give the witness a chance to answer that question so the General would have an answer, I want to point out that is the third time the witness was asked the same question and answered, yes, that's what we can see from this document. So we are really reaching the limits of the utility. Again, he has asked for 7 to 8 hours, it's up to him how to use that. But we've heard the same question three times about whether Alija Izetbegovic gave his consent to have the civilians removed and he has asked that three times.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes, problem of repetition in questioning occurs several times in this courtroom. I think, Mr. Tolimir, this witness is very important for you, you should use him and his knowledge and his recollection as much as possible for your purposes. Go ahead, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Please, Mr. Joseph, tell us was General Smith aware of Alija Izetbegovic's plan set out in this telegram to Hajric? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't answer that. I don't know whether or not General Smith was aware.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. The proposal put forth by Alija Izetbegovic, which he refers to as his plan to move out as many civilians as possible, was it ultimately materialised in the enclave of Zepa? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Tolimir, you are asking me to characterise too many things here as a plan and so forth. I really want to be responsive to you. I really do, I just don't know that I'm really in a position to assist on this. What I'm -- can tell you is, yes, and I've stated, these women and children, yes, they were moved out and your side did not impede that. To the contrary, your side helped by providing vehicles and even though you are not asking me, I'll tell you affirmatively, your side helped and assisted in providing vehicle, sometimes with drivers and all. We had our concerns and our caution, and that's why we were there and why I tried to keep an UNPROFOR soldier, if we could have had enough and spare one on each one, and we tried our best to keep good accountability. But you are taking me into things about Izetbegovic and his plans and things like this which I honestly, General Tolimir, I respectfully don't believe I can shed too much light on.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please, let's look at document 1D00600.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: It's a document sent by Akashi to Kofi Annan, Stoltenberg and Smith at UNPROFOR Sarajevo which sets out the policy of the peace forces and recommendations for the Security Council?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Before we move to this document, I would like to ask you if you were tendering two previous documents you have used and which are not in evidence yet. One is is 1D195 and if I'm not mistaken, and the other is 65 ter 7203. You used them with the witness, are you tendering them?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. For reminding me that, yes, we do wish to tender them into evidence. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: The document 1D195 will be received as an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 1D195 receives number D172, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And the other document, the statement of the witness to the OTP, 65 ter 7203 will be received as well.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 7203 receives number D173, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Carry on, Mr. Tolimir, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Can we look at paragraph 1, line 3.
