It's the second word in line 3 and I'll be quoting Mr. Akashi's words: "I've just concluded a meeting with my senior military and political advisors, and with the UNHCR special envoy, at which a general consensus was reached on the policy that the United Nations Peace Force, UNPROFOR and UNHCR will pursue with regard to Srebrenica in the coming one to seven days." I wanted to read this out because it refers to the policy and to the UNHCR. You mentioned the UNHCR a moment ago in the content of its refusal to carry out the evacuation from Zepa. So this is my question: The policy of the United Nations as set out by Mr. Akashi to Annan and other members of the United Nations which was copied to Sector Sarajevo and Mr. Smith, was it also binding on the UNHCR? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Tolimir, my best answer to this question is I am genuinely not sure whether Akashi had overall authority and direction of UNHCR. It's possible that he did. He is, in this document, is reflecting agreement of UNHCR, but that doesn't necessarily mean that he actually had formal authority, and it's equally possible that UNHCR then and still does in other context retains its independent authority outside of what Mr. Akashi, who is in the DPKO chain, had. So again, I'm not the best witness here. There's others who can shed light on this, but again this document didn't -- was not something that was guiding us in Zepa, in any immediate sense.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. In this document, did Mr. Annan inform all those listed here, including Mr. Smith, about the position of the peace forces, UNPROFOR, and UNHCR, vis-a-vis Srebrenica in the coming period? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: If I'm not mistaken, you were asking if Mr. Akashi informed these people and not Mr. Annan as you are recorded. Thank you. Sir, please, your answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would just like to, again, state that I am not in a position here, as a former member of UNPROFOR, to speak in any authoritative way about what Mr. Akashi was doing and who he was informing and whatnot. My value here is that I was on the ground in Zepa, General Tolimir, you and I were there together, but I -- I understand, if you want to introduce these in evidence, you know, the Court and the Chamber has its procedures for doing that. But I'm really not able to shed much light on this or communication from President Izetbegovic to Hajric anymore than, for example, if there were communication from President Karadzic to the equivalent in Rogatica stating whatever the intentions were with respect to Muslims in Zepa. I couldn't provide any special insight into that communication either, if it were presented into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And thank you, Mr. President. And again, Trial Chamber may not have seen this for a few days, but General Smith is scheduled to testify. We have reserved an entire trial week for his testimony, just to remind everybody that he will be here and available just for the types of questions that -- many of which are being put to this witness, but he will be here for a full week in March, the week of March 21st.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I think we are all aware of that. Thank you very much. I take the opportunity to correct one discussion about a document. 1D195 has not a translation yet, therefore 1D -- sorry, D172 will be marked for identification, pending translation. Please carry on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Thank you to Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Can you please tell us when this document was authored, if you can have a look? Were you in Sarajevo or in Zepa at the time?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was probably en route or in Tuzla at the time, if memory serves. Very soon into that as soon as we anticipated the fall of Srebrenica, I was sent to Tuzla. Whether it was on the 11th of July, I can't say right now.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Since below the date it reads, the policy of the United Nations Peace Force, would you as a political advisor have had to know something about it, and to be acquainted with this document by your superior? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again my role was a civil affairs officer which at times included political advice. We wouldn't necessarily know. The answer is no, we wouldn't necessarily be privy to this specific document but what we would be privy to, we might be privy to it, but we might not be. Absolutely what we would know and what would be communicated to us was a relevant policy decision, so if a decision had been taken and we were in a position to -- that that decision was relevant to us, yes, we would be informed about that. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have page 2 of this document, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: May I put a question to the witness in the meantime. Sir, did you ever see this document which is on the screen now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mr. President, I don't recall this document. It's theoretically possible that I did, but to answer your question, sir, at this time I don't recall this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Can we have the bottom of the document visible because we'd like to look at the last page and then move on to the next page. So I'm quoting from the last line on this page.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: "UNPROFOR shall, with the support of the UNHCR, also try" and can we now have the next page, please. Then page 3, line 1, "try and achieve -- try and reach an agreement with the Bosnian Serbs about providing escorts for all the refugee convoys from Srebrenica to Tuzla." This is my question: Does it not clearly follow from this that UNPROFOR had an obligation to participate in evacuations and policies carried out by United Nations contingents in these areas? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: You'll have to permit me a chance to read this and again I'm not -- now because this is electronic, I'm not able to read the whole document, but if you are referring to, is it paragraph (b), General Tolimir, that I'm supposed to be focusing on?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: The relevant part Mr. Tolimir was quoting from is just in the middle of the page. You see the abbreviation UNPROFOR just in the middle of the page, that is on the bottom of paragraph (b) indeed. "UNPROFOR with the support of UNHCR will also endeavour to reach agreement." Just in the middle of the page. Do you see it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yeah, I do, thank you, that's very helpful. Mr. President. Yes, I do see that, it appears Mr. Akashi, if this is still the Akashi document is assuming an obligation on the part of UNPROFOR and he is anticipating that UNHCR is going to have the support, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Joseph.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation], I do not need this document any longer. Although you can see that it goes on to say about UNPROFOR and UNHCR taking part in evacuations, et cetera, I wish to tender this document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter didn't understand whether Mr. Tolimir wants the document to be admitted or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, the last part of your sentence was not interpreted and recorded. Could you repeat that, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, yes, I wish to tender the document into evidence since the witness said what he had to say about this document also in answer to your question. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, I would like to ask you if you intend to use this document with the witness Rupert Smith? In that case it would be more helpful to use it with that witness and to tender that at that point in time, because obviously from the face of this document, he received a copy of it and I didn't understand this witness to comment on this document. When I asked him, he said he doesn't recall ever having seen it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. But because he said that it is possible that he was acquainted with the document, would it be possible to mark it for identification. This document is relevant for the topic that we have been discussing, the evacuation. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: This is a good proposal. Indeed, it will be marked for identification and may be used at a later time in this trial.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 1D600 receives number D174, marked for identification, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Please carry on, Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Mr. Joseph, during the evacuation of the population, women and children, did you report to your command about the evacuation -- did you report to Sarajevo about the evacuation? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Tolimir, this document is referring to modalities for Srebrenica. Are you asking me about Srebrenica and in Tuzla or are you asking me about when I was in Zepa?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Joseph. We have left that topic behind. We are not going to discuss that document and now we are talking about Zepa. So my question is, did you report to your command about the evacuation from Zepa? That's what I'm asking you about, not the previous document.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: The answer to that is yes, I did as we had means and time to report, affirmative, I -- Viktor and I did make sporadic reports that would have been voice.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, then, can we have 65 ter 7208. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: I want the witness to see what the topic of my questions is going to be. It's a report dated the 26th of July, 1995, drafted by Tony Banbury. While we are waiting for it, yes, we have it, can you tell the Trial Chamber, who is Tony Banbury, what was his function in the UNPROFOR at the time?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Tony was an advisor to -- in Mr. Akashi's cabinet, he was an advisor to Mr. Akashi.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. The first two paragraphs that we can see on the screen say the following: "At around 15.15 today, Ed Joseph called from Zepa (the UNPROFOR political and humanitarian affairs officer) using a French satellite phone. He passed on the following information." And then under number 2 he goes on to say: "The evacuation of the civilian population is proceeding: 24 Serbs buses with approximately 50 people each, and seven UNPROFOR and Serb trucks with similar and smaller numbers are loaded in Zepa, and expected soon to depart for Kladanj. At least one UNPROFOR soldier will travel on each vehicle. The people are not being forced to leave, but decided to do so as part of the total evacuation of the enclave. Those departing are being registered by UNPROFOR political and humanitarian affairs officers to the extent possible. The town's mayor and his staff are also involved in registering the departing population." My question is as follows: Does this document correctly reflect the information you passed to the command that Mr. Tony Banbury was a part of? So he was the chief of protection force of the UN?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: This document does not completely and accurately reflect the full nature of the information that -- that we had on the ground. No, it does not.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Does it reflect the message that you sent from the field to the UNPROFOR staff? Does it reflect the essence of your message? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would say today I doubt that it does in one important respect. In respect of the statistics, I presume that I conveyed that information and that Tony accurately reflected that in the -- in his report. With respect to the point that the people are not being forced to leave, I doubt that that was part of my message. To the contrary, per previous testimony I noted, and this is quite fundamental for the Chamber, that because we were acting without UNHCR, basically in place of UNHCR, because they refused to participate in an operation that they deemed ethnic cleansing, so we, for humanitarian purposes, were forced to do this without the assistance of UNHCR, and I and Viktor had consulted UNHCR as to what -- how does one do this? What are the laws and rules about how you conduct such an operation? And the first thing that they told me, the essential point, they said, is, under humanitarian law, you have to determine the volition that these people are doing so willingly and it's not under duress, they are not being forced to leave. That's what you have to, that's your first obligation. And per my previous testimony, which I understand been entered in now, I said that Viktor and I implemented that. That's what we were implementing. We weren't implementing some deal between Torlak. We were implementing this onward movement, and as we were suggested to do by UNHCR, and the very first thing that Viktor and I did that morning of the 26th of July, 1995, the very first thing we did was start to consult those women who were gathered in the centre of the town and we went one by one to say to them, do you agree to willingly leave and go on the bus, and the first one said yes and the second one until we got past a dozen or so, maybe it was later on than that down there, and then it was not very far, and one of them said after the others had prior to her had said yes, I voluntarily she said, no, I don't go voluntarily, I don't want to go. I want to stay here in my home, but who will protects me? And she began to cry and with that as soon as she began to cry, they all began to cry, and it was very clear to Viktor and me that it was less humanitarian for us to continue to proceed with this inquiry, that was just putting these women who were obviously very distressed to put them under more stress simply to put a tick in a box. It was very, very ample and evident to us that these women were going out and leaving their homes under duress, that this was an overall context of duress in which they feared that if they were to stay alone that they would be in very great risk for themselves and for their children. And that, that is the context. And so this report stating that they were not forced to leave might have a narrow meaning in that there wasn't a person with a bayonet at their back doing it, but it was the overall presence of Serb forces and the fact that they no longer had any -- any defence and were now in the control of Serb forces which put them in extreme apprehension and fear and it was in those circumstances that they boarded those buses and, General Tolimir, I'm confident that you understand what I'm saying.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Before I respond to this, did you give any information to this Tony Banbury about the dilemma of these women or did you tell him what he quoted in his report, did you apprise the UNPROFOR command about the situation with those women in Zepa, about their dilemmas and fears about the pact that the Zepa Brigade was not there anymore? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I probably -- Viktor and I were quite aware of the mental state of agitation of the population and it is likely, we use the word "likely," that we did report that and then further I can recall the specific event that reinforced this viewpoint that we had and that was so plainly evident was when, after the severely wounded men had been evacuated, were being evacuated, there were no buses at that time in the centre, and these women went into a mass panic because they felt that this was the last convoy and that they were going to be left there. They felt that they were going to be abandoned there and this was not the reaction of a population that is sort of, yeah, gee, you know, we'll make it through okay, some of us will go, some of us will stay. No, this was the absolute panic of women who were thinking that they had -- that they were about to miss the last chance to get out and would be left in a situation at the mercy of their adversaries and I'm quite confident that we reported that. Whether -- you have to remember one thing too for Tony. Tony was in Zagreb with Akashi and our main direction of reporting was to Sarajevo and David Harland, so it's possible that Tony may not have gotten that, but this characterization in this report is contrary to what Viktor and I witnessed in Zepa.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Now, what you just said a moment ago, that they first told you they went of their own free will and later that it wasn't the case, and what you told us a little while later that they were afraid they would be left there, isn't that contradictory? What is in the end their will and what are their emotions and how did that influence their behaviour? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Tolimir, that is really a very interesting question and I'm confident that we both know that, having both been in the war there in Bosnia, that not only Muslims, but Serbs also had great fear at times when in a minority situation, and I would say with UNPROFOR we were also very attentive and concerned about that, as did Croats as well. I think we all know that. And for -- I don't think there is a contradiction. If the general understanding of what free will is that one does something in a state of relative choices and one makes rational choices, sure, it's a rational choice to leave your home where your family has lived, and maybe your forefathers, for literally centuries. It's, in some sense, a rational decision to leave that all behind if you believe that if you do not do that you'll lose your life and put your children as well in jeopardy. So I would just turn it back to the Chamber to determine what constitutes free will. All I will tell you is I'm convinced that these women were absolutely terrorised and petrified and their concern was if they remained in that town, their survival was something subject to serious question. I'm quite convinced of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Joseph, does that mean that the VRS was not supposed to disarm the demilitarised zone simply because of the strength of the emotions of the civilian population? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't say that. Those two -- I don't say that. I thought we were addressing ourselves to the question of whether or not the women getting on the bus was free will. I think I said before this question of demilitarisation was a long-standing one, went back to Srebrenica in 1993 with General Morillon, and Zepa and the other safe areas, and I think it's a quite legitimate concern, for the Serbs, of demilitarisation, and I said before that this is -- as to why these safe areas were never fully demilitarised, I said that's a long and lengthy explanation and I think other witnesses can get into that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Judge Nyambe has a question for the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: Thank you. Just some clarification at page, excuse me, at page 58, lines 11 to 12, you have just said, "All I'll tell you is I am convinced that these women were absolutely terrorised and petrified." Can you just elaborate who terrorised these women, in the context of your evidence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Judge Nyambe, for the opportunity to clarify this. What I meant was, and I can give -- I'm grateful for a second reason, in that I can give you a concrete example, why this isn't just inference on our part. What I mean is that they were in a state of apprehension as to -- after the bombardment that had occurred and this is now approaching three -- it is after three plus years of war, that they were in great fear as to what their fate would be were they to remain there seeing many of their kindred leave, that they were in a state of absolute intense anxiety that I would say is terror. I would say they felt terror. And I'll give you the concrete example. In general the -- as I testified, the Serb forces were co-operative and kept their distance from where we were, but occasionally they would come in and at one point there was a Serb military vehicle with a Serb flag, Cetiri S on it that came through and the women absolutely shrieked in horror and fear and recoil from that. So this is another example of this state of very intense anxiety in which they were about what would befall them. And for the accused and his attorney, I just want to emphasise that this might well have been a similar thing for Serb civilians or Croats in a similar situation. And so we know that the fate was not kind to isolated and minority vulnerabilities and we were -- tried to be equally sensitive I think to that for Serbs who might have been in a similar position.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: Thank you for your answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Joseph. While you were in Zepa did you see any soldier or officer who came to the place where civilians were boarding buses and tried to compel anybody to leave Zepa or to interfere with the activities that you and the civilian authorities are engaged in? Thank you?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Tony Banbury calls you, in this document, "political and humanitarian affairs officer". Could you tell us, were you really a political and humanitarian affairs officer? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: And thank you, General Tolimir, for calling attention to that, because that is, in fact, another inaccuracy in this document. I do not recall that such a position existed. We were civil affairs officers, that was our title. Viktor Bezruchenko and I were civil affairs officers. David Harland was senior civil affairs officer, John Ryan was civil affairs co-ordinator. That was our title formally, informally, and I don't ever recall such a term being used and I think it's interesting that it all of a sudden would appear here when the common and constant usage was always civil affairs officer, both formally and informally.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. When we talk about the civil affairs, does that also include political and humanitarian issues in the zone or the region where you were active? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: It does, absolutely. Those were political and humanitarian issues were of course in the writ of civil affairs officers, but I just note that this is inaccurate to use this term and it's not only inaccurate, it's unconventional. It's unusual, and therefore, curious as to why it would appear.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. A moment ago we discussed the situation that arose in Zepa. Are the Serbs to blame for this situation or is it the guilt of the Muslims because they were active in this protected zone that had been accorded to them earlier and they even engaged the Main Staff, so did you have any information that the Muslims were active from within that demilitarised zone? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Tolimir, this is a central question. Unfortunately, I can't answer it, either in the narrow sense and to get into the larger sense as who was really the responsible party we would have to have a longer and wider discussion than I think the Chamber is interested in. I really want you to understand our mindset when Viktor and I went in there. It was operational in nature, operational. We were there with the mindset to effect, to use the term he insists upon, evacuation of the women and children in a safe and humane way as we could and potentially the men of Zepa as well. We were not there briefed or mindful or preoccupied with who had caused whom to be in this situation. That, at that point, this is a crisis situation, and that was not our preoccupation, and of course, addressing that, General Tolimir, we would have to look at many wider issues as to the conduct of the war and the many, many wider issues.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. I showed you a document written by Hajrulahovic in February, sent to his Main Staff, saying that General Mladic is protesting and requesting to demilitarise the zone, saying that he will do it himself, because the Zepa zone is being used for the collection of armaments. Do you remember that? It was today during your today's testimony? While I was conducting my cross-examination today.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry document written by whom?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Mustafa Hajrulahovic, aka Talijan, he sent it to Zepa and also the Chief of Staff in Kladanj. Do you remember that document where General Mladic said he himself will perform the demilitarisation if the UNPROFOR will not demilitarise Zepa?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, it would be helpful to put this document on the screen again to help the witness to recall that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Can we have in e-court 1D195, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: This is now D172 marked for identification. While this will be brought point up, we have to adjourn for the second break and I would like to ask you, Mr. Tolimir, to consider if you are tendering the last document, 65 ter 7208, which is on the list of the Prosecution, and after the break I would like to ask the Prosecution if there's a translation. But that should be considered by both parties during the break. We have to adjourn and resume quarter past 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, please carry on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. The witness requested that he be shown document D172. Could we have it in e-court for his benefit. Now we have it before us and this is the document we discussed this morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: This document was sent by the chief of the intelligence administration on the 17th of February, 1995, to the command post in Kakanj to the -- General Hadzihasanovic personally, and to the Zepa Brigade and we saw this morning that he warns them that the aggressor had forwarded their request to the UNPROFOR, that Zepa be proclaimed a non-demilitarized zone, that's the first sentence, and then in the third paragraph, it says, "On the 16th of February, 1995, the aggressor informed the Sarajevo UNPROFOR command that if Zepa is not proclaimed a non-demilitarized zone that they would begin combat operations within seven days." So my question for you is this: In the meetings that you attended and the Joint Commission meeting the Serb side proposed that UNPROFOR disarm the men who were engaging -- who engaged in combat operations from within the zone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: What is the question, Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: My question, Your Honour, was whether the UNPROFOR command was aware and whether the witness was aware that the army, on several occasions, at various meetings that he attended, the meetings of the joint military commission, demanded that combat operations against the territory where Republika Srpska units were, which were launched from within Zepa, be terminated? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Tolimir, today here on the 1st day of March in 2011, I can't say for sure whether I was aware about this specific demand about attacks from Zepa. I can't. It's possible that I was. It's possible that I was in a meeting and that this came up and I am simply not recalling it now. On the lead-up to your question, you mentioned demilitarized zone again, and I just would call to your attention that not only was I aware that this was a chronic issue, but David Harland and I had proposed our own concept for a demilitarized zone for Zepa. So again I am very acutely aware of the importance of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Since you were aware of how important this issue was, did you know, you and the UNPROFOR headquarters, that Muslims frequently left the territories, the protected areas and launched attacks against Serb units outside of them?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would say this, General Tolimir, we knew that there were often -- that problematic relations; this was a state of war. What I can't tell you and I'm being again as responsive as I can, I cannot tell you whether this was the case in Zepa. To the contrary, I was under the impression that compared to Srebrenica, the Zepa area was a lot more quiet. It's a lot smaller than Srebrenica, and the commander there, Palic, you might have your own opinion as to how he compared to Naser Oric in Srebrenica, my understanding is favourably. But I don't have specific information about the nature of Armija attacks, I'm not saying that they didn't happen, but I really can't shed light on that. And again that was not our preoccupation. We were operational there. We were not in a point of assessing blame. We were trying to save lives at that point.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Very well. Tell us, please, did UNPROFOR commands within enclaves and the headquarters in Sarajevo and Tuzla have information about the military activities launched from within the so-called protected zones of Srebrenica and Zepa?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would presume they would have some information. Whether it would be perfect information, I don't know. Again, UNPROFOR movements in Serb-controlled territory were, as you know, very limited, and therefore the ability to observe might have been constrained, but I presume that there was some information about that.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Now, since we saw this document, could we now see D77 because you have requested it for a number of times now and you said that there were certain restrictions imposed by Serbs in the territory.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation]So could we have D77 in e-court, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Here we have the document before us, it's a UN document.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: The BH command headquarters, forward command headquarters in Sarajevo, 31st January 1995, "Principles for freedom of movement." And then under 1, it says: "These principles define the appropriate procedures regarding freedom of movement as stated in paragraph 5 of the agreement on complete cessation of hostilities signed on the 31st December, 1994. These principles specifically refer to UNPROFOR movements on Serb-held territory." And then it goes on to explain and to say that "UNPROFOR will notify the Serbian army authorities 48 hours in advance of convoy movements and 24 hours for single vehicles." And so on and so forth. In paragraph 3, there is mention of checks and check-points and then if we turn on to the next page, we see that these convoys should have the right of free passage and they should be checked in order to make sure that they weren't carrying weapons and so on. And then under 6, we have evaluation and so on. And we see that this was signed by the representative of the headquarters -- UNPROFOR headquarters, General Briquemont [Realtime transcript read in error "Brinkman"], and on behalf of the Serb army headquarters, I was the person who signed this, because at the time I was the acting chief of staff. Now, tell us, please, were these principles agreed with the VRS or was this just something that the Serb army declared themselves or whether they were -- whether these principles were agreed upon together between the sides?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you, General Tolimir. As you know very well, there were many agreements between UNPROFOR and not only your side, the Armija and the HVO. You know we had many, many agreements. And you know, it's true, this was agreed. This was General Briquemont, by the way, it's misspelled, his last name is misspelled here. Yeah, there were many agreements, but the question is were they implemented, were they respected? And you know it was a regular occurrence that we had great difficulty moving convoys in Serb-controlled -- in and through Serb-controlled territory. But I acknowledge that this a signed agreement with General Briquemont, I acknowledge that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Could they move freely? Could UNPROFOR members move freely across the territory of Republika Srpska without prior notification, and without consent or approval? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm no longer able to see the first page of this, so if you are asking me what does this document provide, I think this document, again I'm going from memory now --

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Go ahead, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As I'm going from memory, it a -- this document appears to require some notice, but whether -- if the question is whether UNPROFOR could move freely across the territory of Republika Srpska without prior notification and consent, no, no, we could not. And often we could not move freely with consent and approval. And when I say we, I'm speaking in general; I'm also thinking of humanitarian convoys and those were you routinely had great difficulty moving and Viktor Bezruchenko and I, in fact, were astonished that we were able to reach Zepa on both occasions, because it was just so unheard of to be able to transit freely across Republika Srpska. That was so rare and so difficult that it was really -- we were really astonished that we actually made it to Zepa.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness be shown the first page of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: And my question for him would be, does that mean that there was an agreement between UNPROFOR and the VRS about the movement of UNPROFOR, the time when those movements can be carried out across Republika Srpska territory?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. If you are asking me to read and state what's in the document, the document in paragraph 2(a) requires that UNPROFOR notification. It does. Did I answer the question? I'm sorry, I meant to answer the question, was I responsive?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I think you answered the question, sometimes it takes some time for finishing the interpretation. Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Joseph, I'd like to show you now a document that's 145 in e-court. Thank you. And we just saw in the previous document that the movements were agreed upon. And my apologies, I made an error, the document I need is D145. Thank you. While we wait for it to come up, let me just say that this is a document from the Main Staff of the Republika Srpska army, the intelligence and security administration. We see that it was drafted on the 24th of June, 1995. In other words, a month before the events in Zepa and Srebrenica, and the document discusses enemy activity, and then, they send the following information, and I quote: "On 23rd June at 0200 hours, a unit of approximately 300 soldiers headed out of Srebrenica led by Mandzic, the commander -- Ibrahim Mandzic, the commander of the 280th Brigade; Vejz Sabic, the commander of the 284th Light Brigade; and his deputy Semso Salihovic; as well as a guide, a man called Zoran Cardakovic, a Muslim. The unit's task was to insert itself that same day at approximately 2000 hours, into the general sector of Ruzina Voda, Han Pijesak municipality. This group is equipped with automatic weapons with a couple of 60-millimetre mortars and some RPGs" and so on. And that was the first paragraph. My question, did the UNPROFOR commands in Zepa and Srebrenica and the headquarters in Sarajevo and Tuzla know that Muslim forces co-ordinated their activities, the Muslim forces in Zepa and Srebrenica, and that they used the territory of the other party in order to launch their activities? We can see that there was mention even of Han Pijesak municipality there. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Tolimir, if I understand correctly, General Smith is going to testify, and I think you'll have a much better witness to attest to what UNPROFOR did and didn't know, than this civil affairs officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. The reason I'm asking you this is the fact that you attended all those meetings of the joint military commissions and especially when General Smith was present and that you actually participated in all of those meetings. Now, if we look at the last paragraph of this document, it says: "Also on the 23rd of June of this year in the evening hours, a company from the Manoeuvre Brigade of 120 persons under the command of Jasarevic was sent to Jovino Brdo and this mission will last five days, during which time, they are to perform reconnaissance in the direction of Jeskovik [phoen] and Jasikovac village is right next to the Main Staff, whereas Peruca is on the Drina near Skelani." Now can we have the next page and I will put the question to you. Are you aware that the only way to get out of Srebrenica with as many troops as mentioned here was through Zepa?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: First, you said because I was present in all the meetings of the joint military commission and that's not true, so I have to challenge the premise here that I was somehow present in all the meetings. I was present in some meetings, but I was not present in all the meetings, and I was brought in to go to Zepa with Viktor, because of this crisis situation and because both he and I had some experience that was useful. But I was not in -- these -- we were civil affairs officers and these are much more in the way of military details. We knew in general and had, sure, conversations with General Smith and his colleagues and his staff in general terms, but these are specific military questions as to the -- what the movements were between Srebrenica and Zepa. I'm not disputing them here, I'm saying you have a much better witness in General Smith to speak to this.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we have D62 shown now.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Let me give you a follow-up question to what you've just said: Would these specific military issues affect the position of the civilians in the enclaves? Thank you. I repeat my question because it was not recorded well. These specific military issues you just referred to, would they affect the position of the civilians in the enclaves of Srebrenica and Zepa? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they would to some degree, and my colleague in Tuzla, Ken Biser, who was the senior civil affairs officer there, he might have been quite aware of these specifics. He might, and he might have taken quite some note of movements and what activities were coming out of Srebrenica and whether or not how much linkage. This witness, however, was not in Tuzla, except during the crisis, and was not in Zepa, except also, in this crisis in July of 1995. So I can't speak to these details.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. I know you were not aware of the details, but you would know how far these issues would affect the entire situation and other matters you spoke of. We have D62 on our screens now, which is an BH Army document produced on the 28th of June, 1995, in other words, two days after the report I referred to earlier on, where they are relating the extent of their combat activities to the Main Staff. And so this is the first time I'm showing you a document that was addressed to the Main Staff but I've been throughout showing you documents that were produced by the Muslims. "Item 1, based on the order by the commander standing commander of the 28th Division of Srebrenica, Major Ramiz Becirovic, strictly confidential, such and such a number, on measures to be taken on the execution of sabotage actions aimed at" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I have to interrupt you. You should slow down while reading, it's very complicated for the interpreters and the court recorder. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: So, "... aimed at inflicting losses on the aggressor in troops and hardware, and in general at turning the Chetnik forces away from Sarajevo." This is my question: Did the UNPROFOR in Sarajevo have knowledge to the effect that orders were issued to the enclave to tie forces away from Sarajevo and about the co-ordinated action taking place between the forces in the enclave and those outside of it? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me say, General Tolimir, this line of questioning if I can address it, yes, I was personally aware that military activity by the Bosnians or Bosniaks, by the Armija, could have serious repercussions for civilians, and as you may know, I was in Bihac in 1994 when General Dudakovic and the 5th Corps made an attack south of Bihac, and then this produced a Serb counter-attack and it had great consequences for the civilian population. So, yes, in principle, I'm definitely aware of that dynamic there during the war in Bosnia-Herzegovina. But I can't speak to these specific elements. I might have been aware of some aspects of the strategy of the Armija with respect to Sarajevo, but those are generally preoccupations for the military, and I'm suggesting that General Smith will be an infinitely better witness than I can on these subjects.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, I'm asking you about this because I wanted to know what your position was, what the prevailing opinion within the command was and you were part of the command. I'll read from the first line of paragraph 2, and then proceed to the last lines: "On receipt of the orders given me by brigade commanders," and I'm moving on to the end of the paragraph, "I decided to proceed as follows:" Next paragraph: "Form a number of sabotage groups, of between a squad to reinforced platoon strength, and dispatch them deep into the temporarily occupied territory for the purpose of inflicting on the aggressor as high losses as possible, in terms of troops and equipment and tying him down, with the new forces he requires, across a swathe of over 20 kilometres wide." And then he proceeds to speak of the axes of attacks for these various groups. And can we turn to the next page, while I'm putting my question to you. Does it arise from the documentation of the BH Army that they carried out attacks out of the protected areas roughly a month before the start of the offensive launched by the VRS for the view to demilitarising them?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, genuinely sorry, General Tolimir. It's just not useful for me to address these issues. This documentation purports to be whatever it purports to be, and I'm just not in a position here now to amplify on this. I am not, and I'll say it again, I am not disputing the thrust of what you are saying. If you are trying to suggest that the Armija was making attacks, I'm not here telling you that you are wrong. I'm simply saying that this witness is not really in a position to shed light on this.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. We have the relevant page now. It says that the report was signed by Commander, Colonel Avdo Palic. Let's read the first line where it says, "About 40 Chetniks were killed." You can see it in paragraph 3 in English. "About 40 Chetniks were killed and dozens were wounded, a significant quantity of infantry weapons were seized." Would any side, which had granted an area the status of a protected zone, have the obligation to protect civilians and others present in an area if they came under attack from a protected zone? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: If your question is about whether or not Republika Srpska had the right to protect its civilians in a time of war, I say, yes, Republika Srpska had the right to protect its civilians in a time of war. Whether or not, whether or not they were under attack from a safe area. Even if they were attacked from an area that wasn't a safe area, they would have the right to defence. Now, it's a different question as to what transpired with respect to the safe area in Zepa and what was in the run-up to that and whether -- which side lived up to its obligations and which side did not live up to its obligations. That's, I think, a very interesting inquiry but unfortunately I can't help with that inquiry because I arrived in Zepa during a crisis with a specific humanitarian role. So I'm not disputing this, General Tolimir, but I'm -- I don't think I'm assisting the Chamber here on this line.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Joseph.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have 1D28 shown.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: You've just said that it's a different question as to what transpired. When we see the title, we'll see that it says that it's a chronology of the events of the break-through of the 28th Division of the land forces, sent by the 2nd Corps of the BH Army to the commander, General Rasim Delic. And there is contained a full chronology of these events seen from the perspective of the Muslim documentation. It also refers to the period of time you spent in Tuzla.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we show page 6, please, to see the relevant portion.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Here we see a summary report toward the end where Rasim Delic in the portion containing seven bullet points, or rather eight, I am sorry, and that is paragraph 5, where he speaks of the various units, their places of deployment and their passage through the corridor to Tuzla at the time when you were there. Since I don't have much time left, this is my question: Were you told at a time you were in Tuzla that the units of the BH Army that were freeing or working their way through the VRS-held territory arrived ultimately in the free territory? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: If my memory is correct, General Tolimir, I believed that we were told, I think there was even a report that was shown that indicated that some of the men did, indeed, arrive safely in the territory. Of course, I don't think I'm introducing anything new. I think it's a matter of record that we know that several thousand Muslim men were killed in Srebrenica and never made it anywhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Did the several thousand ultimately arrive, or was it the case that they actually fought their way through to the free territory with the support of the BH Army troops? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: There's so much contained in this question that I hesitate even to answer and I'm confused as to the premise and as to the meaning, I don't know who you were referring to in several thousand. We know, I believe it's a fact that is accepted is that several thousand Muslim men and boys, that is, at least teenagers, perished in Srebrenica in circumstances that I think are also well documented and I'm not a fact witness to them, so I'm not even going to state that here. But if you are asking me was I aware that some Muslim men made their way, I believe I was aware that some did indeed make their way. Whether they fought their way or not, I wasn't present and I don't recall what the reports said. The reports might have spoken to that and maybe they were silent on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, we must come to an end for today. I would like to remind you before the last break I asked you about the document you used with the witness, 65 ter 7208. This is not yet on the 65 ter exhibit list but used by the Defence, so that I take it there's no objection to add this document to the 65 ter exhibit list; is that correct, Mr. Gajic?

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, we don't have any difficulty with this document. I think it was on our list, but under a different 1D number, so we would like to tender it into evidence as a Defence exhibit. The Prosecution did not use the document with this witness, so we believe that it should be assigned a D number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Gajic, can you give us the 1D number or whatever on your list? The problem today is that several times documents were used not included in the list of the Defence. Do you have the number? It would be helpful.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not at present. I think that in the most recent list it was struck off, because it had previously been contained on the Prosecution list and the practice was that in the case of the documents contained on the OTP list, we would not place them on ours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, the document remains on the Defence list of exhibits. It's 1D00608. It's on page 4 of their list. We have no objection to the -- obviously to the document going in and to follow up on my suspended oral motion of yesterday, we would move that it be added to the 65 ter list of exhibits and we don't care what number it gets, whether it's the 65 ter number from the Prosecution or the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Does this document have a translation?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: No, it does not. It's been submitted for translation though, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. This document will be added to the 65 ter list of the Prosecution and will be received as a Defence exhibit but only marked for identification pending translation.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This document receives number D175 marked for identification, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Even if documents are listed in the Prosecution's exhibit list, it would be helpful for the Chamber and the other party to include these documents to the list of potential exhibits used during cross-examination. We have to come to an end for today. We will adjourn and resume tomorrow in the afternoon at 2.15 in this courtroom. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 2nd day of March, 2011, at 2.15 p.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 7.02 p.m.
